title: Rumor Has It
full_review:
What if the 1967 film "The Graduate" had been based on reality? And older-woman seductress Mrs. Robinson and preppy young Benjamin Braddock's affair were to have repercussions years later?

Such is the promising, but ultimately disappointing, premise of "Rumor Has It..." (Warner Bros.), which boasts a good cast but a fairly unsavory story.

Sarah Huttinger (Jennifer Aniston) is a journalist, eking out a living as an obituary writer for The New York Times. She's engaged to marry boyfriend Jeff (Mark Ruffalo), but has doubts about her commitment. When the film opens, they're flying home for her sister's (Mena Suvari) wedding in Pasadena, Calif. (On the plane, they try to make love in the restroom with disastrous results, the first of the film's several unfunny gags.)

On her home turf, Sarah feels an odd disconnect from her family. When she learns from her grandmother, Katharine (Shirley MacLaine), that her late mother once had an affair just before marrying Sarah's father (Richard Jenkins), Sarah resolves to track the man down.

The titular "rumor" -- which motivates Sarah in her quest of self-discovery -- is that "The Graduate" (first a book in 1963, by the way) was in fact inspired by her own family, and that Katharine was the "Mrs. Robinson" of the story, which would have made Sarah's mother Benjamin's love interest. If the rumor is true, this man could be Sarah's father.

Sarah finds her mother's lover, Beau (Kevin Costner), now a famous Internet billionaire, lecturing in San Francisco, and confronts him with her suspicions that she may be his daughter.

He accepts her charges with dramatically unbelievable equanimity, and he convinces her that this could not be so -- because he's been sterile for years because of "blunt testicular trauma" sustained during a football game. He charms her off her feet, and before you know it, she's waking up in bed beside him.

Misunderstandings and conflicted emotions follow, including the titillating (to Sarah) possibility that she has indeed just slept with her own father. Though, of course, all is set right by the end, the setup leaves a distinctly bad taste.

Aniston is adequate in the lead role, but her repeatedly wrong assumptions and actions, at least as written, make her character more tiresome than appealing. Costner and Ruffalo are fine as the two men in her life. MacLaine's feisty and still glamorous grandmother role is less juicy than her recent grandmother turn in "In Her Shoes," while Jenkins and Suvari do good work as the father and younger sister.

Director Rob Reiner handles this material capably, and there's even a sentimental pro-family ending, but it fails to eradicate much of the squishy morality throughout.

The film contains a vaguely incestuous theme, a permissive view of premarital sex, sexual situations, some profanity, crude language and expressions, drug references, a condom reference and partial nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
